items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The saxophones were Marshall Royal, Frank Wess, Ernie Wilkins, Charlie Fowlkes on baritone, and myself.

ctx.x: When you joined the band who was there at that point?

In the trumpet section were Joe Newman, a gentleman by the name of Paul Campbell -- they used to call him Uncle Cam -- Wendell Culley, a very distinguished looking and acting person from Worchester, Mass., who spoke perfect English and was a gentleman and always wore a suit and tie. I said Joe Newman, right? The lead trumpeter was a person called Renauld Jones. Trombones were Henry Coker, Benny Powell, and the composer-arranger Johnny Mandel. The saxophones were Marshall Royal, Frank Wess, Ernie Wilkins, Charlie…
So at that point Jimmy Wilkins had left the band?

items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: Charlie Fowlkes... pulled my bandstand out from in front of me... everybody in the band broke up

ctx.x: Yeah, I was going to bring that up.

I lost my dress shoes. We had a brown and tan tux, and I lost my brown dress shoes. Misplaced them, they weren’t lost, maybe Barracuda got them or something. But anyway, by concert time, I had no dress shoes. And with this brown and tan tuxedo, I had some blue and white sneakers. So it came time for me to take a solo, a big solo. On short solos, one might stand up in front of one’s stand and just play eight measures and sit down. But on long, extended solos, you always came out to the microphone. Well with these…
Yeah. There was another time, you remember Titus Turner?

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: the saxophone section at that time was excellent with Marshall Royal playing lead, Frank Wess playing either alto or the other tenor, and Charlie Fowlkes playing baritone.

ctx.x: Did you go through a period of trying to adjust your style, or feel that you needed to adjust your style to play what was required or to fit the Basie band and still satisfy your need for bop?

reading the music, no problem reading and interpreting the music, and the saxophone section at that time was excellent with Marshall Royal playing lead, Frank Wess playing either alto or the other tenor, and Charlie Fowlkes playing baritone. The second alto chair was the only chair that just fluctuated all throughout the entire time I was there.
